THE HUMAN ATLASES · DEEP DIVE

Asia and the Pacific: the other shores of the voyages

Follow the voyages beyond the edge of one regional map. A departure port, an island stop and a return anchorage are parts of the same journey, with the same evidence and the same limits on what can be reconstructed.

This directory connects the existing voyage catalogue across regional guides. It does not add speculative stages or change the shared movie. Representative mapped anchors introduce the area; the complete dated regional list follows below.

One journey across several regions

The dated lists retain each itinerary’s original descriptions. A documented landfall, a roadstead stay and a passage offshore are different kinds of evidence. Where the source leaves a gap, a linking animation is an illustration rather than a recovered daily ship track. [1] [2] [3]

Read departures and returns together

The same port can occur more than once in a journey, and several expeditions can share a harbor. Keeping those visits separate makes it possible to follow preparation, outbound movement and return without turning a port into one timeless event. [1] [2] [3]

3. Archival Coverage, Monsoon / Seasonal Constraints & Limits of Sea-Lane Maps

Historical route lines connecting Batavia roadstead, Tidore: surviving ships, Mactan: Magellan’s death aggregate recurring seasonal sailing tracks, diplomatic dispatches, and coastal provisioning harbors documented in Asia and the Pacific: the other shores of the voyages rather than claiming every vessel followed identical GPS coordinates in every year. [1]

Unequal archival survival—where European admiralty logs or monumental stone harbors outnumber wooden dhow, outrigger, and domestic reed-papyrus records—makes comparative archaeological shipwrecks and bilingual inscriptions essential for reading ocean history evenly. [2]

Schouten and Le Maire · Eendracht around Cape Horn to Jacatra

Eendracht (called Unitie in the English account) sailed with Hoorn from the Netherlands to Patagonia. After Hoorn burned at Puerto Deseado, Eendracht passed the strait between Tierra del Fuego and Isla de los Estados and rounded Cape Horn. The Pacific and East Indies stages end at Jacatra, where the VOC seized the ship. The return aboard Amsterdam is a separate itinerary.

Follow this journey on the shared map ↗

  1. Tafahi · Cocos Island anchorage · 1616-05-11 – 1616-05-13

    The account records trade, Dutch gunfire and casualties. Its accusations against islanders are the voyagers’ interpretation, not a neutral account of intentions. The following movement is not reconstructed.

    Read the linked evidence
  2. Futuna and Alofi · Hoorn Islands sighting · 1616-05-19

    Sighting anchor only. The following days of provisioning and exchanges are described in the source; no exact first anchorage coordinate is asserted. The following movement is not reconstructed.

    Read the linked evidence
  3. Ternate approaches · 1616-09-17

    A dated approach reference, not an assertion of the exact anchoring hour or arrival berth. The Pacific islands and New Guinea coast between anchors remain explicit gaps. The following movement is not reconstructed.

    Read the linked evidence
  4. Jacatra roadstead · Eendracht seized · 1616-10-28 – 1616-11-01

    Original shipboard date retained. The account then records skipping a day to reconcile the westward circumnavigation with local reckoning. Eendracht’s voyage ends here; the return is on other ships. The following movement is not reconstructed.

    Read the linked evidence

Schouten · Amsterdam return from Java

After Eendracht was seized, Schouten and Jacob Le Maire boarded Amsterdam in the homebound fleet of Joris van Spilbergen. Le Maire died during the return. These anchors follow Amsterdam, not the separate Zeeland and not Eendracht.

Tasman: documented New Zealand coastal phase, 1642–1643

A short documented phase of the Heemskerck and Zeehaen voyage. It does not reconstruct the Mauritius, Tasmania, Tonga, Fiji or return legs. Tasman’s crews observed inhabited Māori coasts; the dated anchors are ship observations, not landings.

Follow this journey on the shared map ↗

  1. West coast of South Island, offshore · 1642-12-13

    Te Ara chronology, 13 December 1642. Latitude is reported; longitude is a broad modern anchor south of Cape Foulwind.

  2. Mohua / Golden Bay · 1642-12-18 – 1642-12-19

    First contact between Māori and Europeans, 18–19 December 1642. Encounter with Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri; four Dutch crew were killed on 19 December. Exact anchorage is not asserted.

    Read the linked evidence
  3. Three Kings / Manawatāwhi offshore · 1643-01-05 – 1643-01-06

    Te Ara chronology, 4–6 January 1643. Boats attempted to obtain water; ships anchored nearby and left New Zealand on 6 January. No landing is asserted.

Alexei Chirikov’s St. Paul · independent North Pacific voyage

St. Paul separated from Bering’s St. Peter and reached the southeast Alaskan coast independently. Two boat parties disappeared after approaching shore. The ship returned through the Aleutians with many men suffering from scurvy. Dates retain the published Russian Old Style convention.

Follow this journey on the shared map ↗

  3. Petropavlovsk harbor, return · 1741-10-12

Cook’s Resolution and Discovery · Hawaiʻi, Pacific coast and Arctic

The ships surveyed from Hawaiʻi to Nootka Sound, Alaska and the Arctic pack edge. The crew traded with Indigenous communities along the route. This track ends at Cook’s death, with the crews’ later voyage under Clerke and Gore mapped as separate Clerke and Gore journeys.

Clerke’s Resolution and Discovery · return to the Arctic

After Cook’s death, Clerke led a second attempt through Bering Strait. Ice blocked the northern passage. His last illness ended off Kamchatka on 22 August; the next dated port visit belongs to the surviving expedition under Gore.

Robert McClure · HMS Investigator
